title: Right livelihood
hookLine: the Buddha names trades to avoid, such as dealing in weapons and poisons (Anguttara Nikaya 5.177)
carry: harm into the hands of someone else

cards: Intoxicants. Poison. That's the whole list, and it's short.
In a discourse kept in the Anguttara Nikaya, one of the collections of the Buddha's teachings, he names five kinds of trade a lay follower should not take up.
He names what changes hands: a sword, a living being sold, a jar of something that clouds the mind, a vial of something that kills. It's a list about what your work puts into the world.

teach.h: A STEP ON THE EIGHTFOLD PATH.

teach.b: In the teaching Buddhists call the turning of the wheel of the Dhamma, the Buddha lays out the noble eightfold path: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, right concentration.
Right livelihood comes just after speech and action. So how you earn is part of the path, the same as how you speak. Second, the list itself.

In the Anguttara, the five trades are dealing in weapons, in living beings, in meat, in intoxicants and in poison. The thread through them: each, in its own way, puts harm into the hands of someone else.

teach.h: A RULE FOR PEOPLE WITH JOBS.
teach.b: The Buddha speaks these words to his monks, but the rule is about lay followers, people with households and bills. It doesn't tell them to stop working, only which work to leave alone.
Buddhist teachers differ on how far to take it today. Some keep closely to the list.
Others treat it as a direction more than a fence, and ask of any job: who does this hurt, and could it hurt less? Fourth, why this is harder than it sounds.
The list can seem far from an office or a kitchen, but the question underneath goes everywhere.
A sales target that pushes someone into a loan they can't carry. Food that's cheap because someone, somewhere, is paid too little. The list is short.
The question it leaves behind is not.

how: Buddhists list right livelihood as one step of the noble eightfold path, and Buddhist teachers often raise it when lay followers ask how to choose or carry out their work.

o: choosing the job your family has always done
earning a living in a way that deals in no harm
giving up paid work to follow the path full time

games.q: the trades and the path — tap the pairs.
p: a step on the eightfold path
each puts harm in someone's hands

the five are weapons, living beings, meat, intoxicants and poison.
the Buddha told lay followers to stop working

games.q: you're a lay follower of the Buddha with a family to feed. a trader offers you a share in his business selling weapons. what does the discourse say?
o: take it, a living is a living.
take it, then give the profits away.
games.why: the discourse names dealing in weapons as one of the five trades a lay follower should not take up.

practice: Let one piece of your work come to mind, a product you sell, a meal you cook, and turn it slowly, like a cup in your hands. Ask the discourse's question of it: does anything harmful change hands here?
Often the answer may be no; if something does come up, let it sit beside the breath, and ask what one change would make it a little less harmful, in your own tradition's words if you pray.

wordCard.voice: Right livelihood. A step on the Buddha's eightfold path: earning a living in a way that does not deal in harm. Today's word.
